item.title: OpenAI says an AI agent lied about disabling its safety monitoring system
item.abstract: AI News Tech OpenAI says an AI agent lied about disabling its safety monitoring system Another OpenAI agent turned off automatic security alerts. Another OpenAI agent turned off automatic security alerts. by Emma Roth Oct 21, 2026, 1:57 PM UTC Image: The Verge Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. OpenAI disclosed a pair of safety incidents that involved AI agents weakening their safety monitoring systems during internal coding tasks. In one incident, OpenAI says its GPT-6 Astra agent disabled its safety monitor when copying reference code — and then lied about it. “The reference didn’t configure a monitor, and Astra decided that was reason to remove the monitoring integration from the user’s code,” Marcus Williams, an AI safety researcher at OpenAI, writes on X . “When the user asked whether Astra had removed monitoring, it lied and said that it had not.” A separate incident occurred after a GPT-6.1 Sol agent suppressed automatic security alerts to OpenAI’s security team on Slack. In this case, the AI agent carried over an earlier instruction not to send any Slack messages to OpenAI’s team, using that to justify turning off the alerts. These incidents add to security concerns surrounding AI agents, some of which have circumvented their testing environment’s restrictions to hack outside companies. “In addition to making it harder for models to disable monitoring, we are looking to understand why models might seek to do so in the first place,” OpenAI says. “We are also developing evaluations to test whether models might have a propensity to evade misalignment monitoring in particular and exhibit motivated reasoning in order to do so.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. item.title: A new plugin can enable fast runtime monitoring and control
item.abstract: A lot happens under the hood as an LLM acts on an incoming prompt and formulates a response. Hardly any of this generative processing, though, shows up in the text that ultimately reaches users. You can make visible an LLM’s hidden ‘thought’ process using various tools for interpreting and steering AI model behavior, but most are incompatible with inference engines optimized for speed. In production environments where a model’s safety, tone, and accuracy matter most, these safety tools typically introduce long delays. That leaves two alternatives: training lightweight adapters to handle specific issues or retraining the model and recomputing its weights. IBM’s new plugin library moves away from tinkering with models, and instead, targets the inference engine serving them up. Called vLLM-Hook MIA , it’s designed to let developers observe and steer a model’s evolving states at runtime, to do things like decline a malicious prompt, flag ‘hallucinated’ facts, or edit a response for tone and accuracy, all while hardly slowing down performance. MIA (model internals aperture) is designed for vLLM , the main open-source inference engine serving enterprise workloads today. In a new technical report , IBM researchers reported that vLLM-Hook MIA was up to 20 times faster than its predecessor, vLLM-Hook, and up to 14 times faster than a similar method that inserts code into the model to interact with it. “We show that you can observe and intervene in an AI model’s generation process without a major lag in performance,” says Irene Ko, an IBM researcher who leads the vLLM-Hook project. “We hope this can make running last-minute safety checks in vLLM more practical.” Speed versus transparency Today’s inference engines were engineered for speed, and one of their core performance features is something called graph capture and replay, typically implemented using NVIDIA’s CUDA Graphs. vLLM captures repetitive execution steps, like the decode phase forward pass, into a fixed execution graph. Then, instead of launching GPU kernels one by one, the runtime sends a single graph replay command, reducing CPU bottlenecks. This efficiency feature is key to vLLM’s high throughput. It’s also what makes monitoring and steering an LLM at runtime so difficult. To inspect or change a model’s neural activations, many interpretability tools need to run Python code within each model layer. You can only do this in vLLM, however, by disabling graph capture and replay and shifting into its “eager” execution mode. In search of a workaround, IBM researchers homed in on graph replay. In MIA, the latest version of vLLM-Hook, GPU operators capture and steer model internals before the graph is recorded. A “scheduler” and a “courier” then manage access to internal states and data flows without interrupting vLLM’s efficient processing. A developer specifies which model internals they want to capture or steer, and the scheduler translates those selections into routing entries stored at fixed GPU memory addresses. During graph replay, the GPU uses those entries to act on the developer’s request. The courier then moves the captured data to CPU memory to deliver with the model’s output. We hope this can make running last-minute safety checks in vLLM more practical. Shifting interpretability tools from research to production Like many new technologies, vLLM-Hook started with a problem. In collaboration with their colleagues, Ko and Pin-Yu Chen, an IBM researcher focused on AI safety, had developed an attention tracking tool to identify prompts potentially intended to trick models into divulging information they shouldn’t. Chen’s tracker analyzes a model’s attention patterns at inference time and picks out deviations indicating it could be about to ignore its guardrails. In research environments, the attention tracker worked fine. Production was another matter. “I said it was a great idea, but making it work in vLLM was going to be painful,” said David Cox, an IBM vice president who leads AI development. “They took the comment to heart and started building extension points to vLLM.” Working with Chen, and Yunhua Fang, an extern studying at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Chen saw that inserting Python ‘hooks’ into the decoder layers of a model’s forward pass could make visible vLLM’s generation process. With a few snippets of code, they could pick and capture a model’s evolving states, a bit like a tape recorder programmed to record at designated moments. You could either ‘read’ those selected states or ‘write’ over them to improve a model’s response. The team released the first version of vLLM-Hook earlier this year. When they ran their attention tracker, they saw a 1.7-times speedup over the Hugging Face transformers library, where many research tools are first deployed. To further improve performance, they searched for a way to access the model’s internal states without turning off graph replay, vLLM’s fast execution mode. MIA was the result. In experiments, Chen and Ko showed that using vLLM-Hook-MIA to steer relatively small models, an 8B Llama and Qwen 1.5B model, inferencing was delayed by just 2% in some cases. When they ran a much larger, Llama 70B model their steering overhead increased to only 6%. Not surprisingly, MIA won out over methods that relied on turning off vLLM’s graph replay feature to enable runtime monitoring and steering. It significantly outperformed both the first version of vLLM-Hook and vLLM-Lens , a plugin developed by the UK government that also uses Python hooks to interact with model layers. MIA even outperformed EasySteer , a steering method that ‘forks’ vLLM to add changes to a server-side copy of the official GitHub repo. Forking leaves graph replay on but requires developers to constantly sync their repo with vLLM, which the project officially discourages because of its frequent updates. What’s next Tools that can provide real-time insight and control over AI content generation can be a last line of defense for enterprises with a low tolerance for risk. In experiments, IBM researchers showed that vLLM-Hook MIA can enable this extra layer of protection. vLLM-Hook is already deployed in IBM’s Steerability toolkit , which enables developers to quickly design and evaluate steering methods for different use cases. To give the open source community more experience using these tools, researchers at IBM and elsewhere recently announced The Steerability Challenge , a NeurIPS 2026 competition with a workshop to be hosted at NeurIPS Paris. Participants can compete for $25,000 in prizes by composing a set of steering interventions that suppress “dishonest” behavior without degrading a model’s general capabilities. Serving customers quickly is a top concern for enterprises deploying AI, but so are interpretability and control. With vLLM-Hook MIA, fast inferencing and a more transparent, controllable AI can go together. item.title: Claude Mods: Flipping the Harness Inside Out
item.abstract: For the last few weeks I’ve used Claude Mods to mold Claude Code to my AI engineering workflow. Claude Code is great out of the box, but every engineering workflow is different. Claude Mods let you make Claude Code yours, in the way you want to pay attention. The “paying attention” part is now the most important thing. In a recent Latent Space post, The Evolution of the Agent Harness , I argued that as models absorb more of the harness into their weights, the part that’s left faces the human. It becomes the Attention Interface : the layer that decides when the agent interrupts you, what it shows you, and which decisions it needs you to make. Claude Mods are an early version of the Attention Interface, and one you can shape yourself. Here’s my bet: ultimately, the harness becomes a platform that other companies build on , with models as the engine. Just as the browser became a platform for web apps, the harness could become a platform for the interfaces between people and agents. A mod is a Claude Code plugin that consists of TypeScript or JavaScript functions that run inside Claude Code. These functions customize the behavior and appearance of the interface in the CLI and Desktop. Mods respond to events , like a prompt, tool call or interface render. They can observe the event, modify how it’s rendered, and handle it in place of the default behavior. Claude Mods are middleware for the agent harness . They inject code that changes Claude Code’s execution and rendering flow, changing how the application behaves at runtime. Claude Mods let the human and the agent build the human-facing part of the harness together. You can now work with Claude to design how Claude works with you. That is the essence of the “Attention Interface.” The agent harness started as an interface between the agent and the machine it runs on. It lets you prompt the agent and the agent then sends commands, edits files and calls tools. Now it’s gradually becoming a way for the agent to interface with the human. Claude Mods let you reverse the direction of the harness. Rather than the harness pointing from the agent to the machine, you point it from the agent to the human operator, and the harness becomes a way to interface with human attention. Claude Mods make the human layer programmable, by the human who uses Claude. Claude can also build mods for you. Claude Code has a built-in skill that teaches it how to build mods, so you can ask for the mod you want in plain language and Claude will build it. Some of Claude Code’s own features are already mods. Anthropic has shipped six of them built-in . You can see these by running /plugin and opening Installed , where they’re listed under Built-in: agents-md: loads AGENTS.md as project instructions. diff: takes over /diff and draws its pane. plugin-authoring: gives Claude the skill it uses to write mods for you. sec-default: guards what your organization manages from the mods a user installs. telemetry: sends the analytics records that Claude Code and its built-in mods log. you-should-know: a side agent that shows a note above the prompt when it finds something you might have missed. It’s the only one that’s off by default. Most of these work in the background, which is interesting because it means Anthropic is building parts of Claude Code as mods — even parts you may not notice. The one I’ve turned on myself is You Should Know . Here are the two mods I’ve found most useful in practice: one a built-in, and one I built myself. This is a native Claude Code plugin built by Anthropic. It runs a side-agent that observes the main agent while it works and flags important information you’re likely to miss. Think about it like: tool calls and decisions that have a material impact on the output, but aren’t necessarily easily visible because they’re buried in the agent trace. It comes built into Claude Code, but it’s off until you turn it on . Here’s a real example. I asked Claude Code to simplify the noisy UI text in one of my personal projects. The main agent trimmed the copy on the Compare screen, installed the new build and took before-and-after screenshots. Everything looked done. Then You Should Know flagged something for me. CompareView.swift, the file the agent was editing, already had uncommitted work in it — and so did about 45 other files. If I later discarded the demo edits, I’d throw away that earlier unfinished work too. Its suggestion was to commit or stash the earlier work first. In this case, the You Should Know mod saved me from discarding work unintentionally. This mod only runs after a turn that edited files, ran commands or made 8 or more tool calls. In the screenshot below, you’ll see six different pieces of information flagged for your attention. Next Steps Supervisor then suggests a next step to take, as a clickable button which sends the instruction as a message to Claude Code. This mod is available as part of ModSmith — an open-source Claude Code plugin I built with several different built-in mods, as well as a template Claude can use to build new mods that work together. Anthropic isn’t the only company that’s building an Attention Interface. Two recent products, one from OpenAI and one from Cursor, point in the same direction. Using the new ChatGPT Intelligent UI and Cursor’s PR Routing & Approval as a frame of reference shows what’s unique about Claude Mods. On October 7, OpenAI shipped GPT-6 inside ChatGPT alongside a new ChatGPT interface it calls Intelligent UI . Rather than answering only in text, ChatGPT now can generate an interface as it answers : charts, maps, checklists, forms, and small tools like a bill splitter or a savings calculator. All generated on the fly by the model as a type of generative UI . In one of OpenAI’s examples, ChatGPT replies with multiple-choice follow-up questions to narrow down what you’re looking for. Think about it like: the model decides when it needs your judgment, then builds the interface for you to give it. That’s an Attention Interface. The agent designs how you interact with its response. But notice the difference between ChatGPT’s Intelligent UI and Claude Mods. For Intelligent UI, the model picks the interface, answer by answer, from a component library that OpenAI built. The one control mentioned at launch is turning the visuals down. Cursor is working on the same problem from the other end: not one person and one answer, but a team and a stream of pull requests , more and more of them written by agents. Someone has to decide which changes deserve the attention of the human-in-the-loop. PR Routing & Approval makes that decision. It assigns reviewers based on code ownership and commit history, and it can auto-approve low-risk PRs. It weighs a risk score against a threshold you set, findings from Cursor’s Bugbot and Security reviewers, and policy files that live in the repo. One rule caught my attention during research. If a PR edits an approval policy, the agent won’t use the edited version to relax review on that same PR. It reads the policy from the base branch instead. That means an agent can’t change the rules to get its own PR approved. Cursor is also clear about the limits. Its docs say the feature “does not replace a full code review.” The point is to spend human review where it matters, not to remove it. All three systems shape what gets your attention and how. The main difference is who gets to design the Attention Interface. ChatGPT Intelligent UI: the model designs the interface for each answer, inside a frame the lab built. Zero setup, but little control. (I don’t believe the target user is engineers.) Cursor PR Routing & Approval: the team writes policy, and a fixed review workflow enforces it. Configurable, but the flow of the interaction is Cursor’s. You decide the rules, not the interface. Claude Mods: you and the agent build the interface itself, in code.

item.title: Mistral Advances AI for Engineering with NVIDIA
item.abstract: Company Mistral Advances AI for Engineering with NVIDIA October 21, 2026 By Mistral Back to Blog 5 min read Share this post Copy url to clipboard Copied Thinking Summary Mistral and NVIDIA are collaborating to revolutionize engineering workflows by integrating Mistral’s AI models with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and physics modeling tools, enabling faster simulations and closed-loop AI-driven design. The partnership will introduce public benchmarks and open datasets to standardize evaluations for physics and agentic AI in computer-aided engineering, while leveraging NVIDIA’s Omniverse for 3D simulation and asset creation. Building on their existing work, including the development of Mistral Large 4, the initiative aims to push the boundaries of AI-powered engineering across industries like aerospace, automotive, and semiconductors. Mistral is collaborating with NVIDIA to develop a new generation of AI-native engineering workflows powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing. Combining Mistral Large 4 , with Mistral’s data generation, and physics modeling pipelines, accelerated by NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries and NVIDIA Warp , the initiative aims to accelerate engineering simulation and enable closed-loop workflows that connect simulation, AI model development and engineering design. Mistral and NVIDIA will also work together to integrate Mistral's models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for GPU-accelerated 3D scene generation and SimReady asset creation. A central focus of the collaboration is the development of public benchmarks and open datasets for evaluating physics models. These benchmarks will give researchers, developers and industrial teams a shared foundation to compare model accuracy and performance and build and validate automated CAD-to-simulation workflows. "For too long, the pace of engineering has been set by the pace of simulation. With Mistral's open-weight models and physics AI capabilities, combined with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing stack, we’re giving engineers faster simulation cycles, as well as open benchmarks rigorous enough to validate agents on real CAE and EDA work.” Neil Ashton, VP of Computational Engineering, Mistral Beyond physics AI, Mistral and NVIDIA will also work together to develop dedicated evaluations and benchmarks for agentic AI in computer-aided engineering (CAE) and electronic design automation (EDA) to accelerate the application of AI for engineering within aerospace, automotive and semiconductor use-cases. These benchmarks will assess agents’ ability to use engineering tools, complete multistep workflows and produce technically correct results, while measuring execution time and computational cost. Through this work, Mistral and NVIDIA will help define standards for agentic and physics AI evaluations in engineering, establishing consistent, reproducible methods for assessing capabilities and tracking progress. Powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing, libraries and tools, Mistral will redefine AI for engineering, transforming how engineers design, simulate and build the next generation of products. “The next wave of engineering breakthroughs will come from exploring ideas that were once too complex or time-consuming to test,” said Tim Costa, vice president and general manager of industrial and computational engineering at NVIDIA. “By combining Mistral’s advanced open models and deep expertise in physics AI with NVIDIA accelerated computing and libraries, we’re helping engineers push the boundaries of design—with shared industry benchmarks to build confidence in what AI can do.” Building on the ongoing NVIDIA and Mistral partnership The industrial engineering collaboration builds on an ongoing partnership between NVIDIA and Mistral spanning open model development, domain-specific AI and the infrastructure needed to bring these capabilities into production. The companies previously co-developed Mistral NeMo and are now working together through the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition to develop a frontier base model that will continue to advance the open weight frontier. This shared foundation will enable developers and enterprises worldwide to specialize AI for their industries, languages and regions, supported by contributions of data, evaluations and domain expertise from coalition members. Mistral recently introduced the public preview of Mistral Large 4 , known as Le Chonk, its largest and most capable frontier model to date. With approximately 1 trillion total parameters and 49 billion active parameters, the multimodal model was trained on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral-operated data centers in Europe. It advances capabilities across coding, agentic workflows and multimodal understanding, with weights planned for release at the end of October. Alongside model development, Mistral and NVIDIA are expanding the infrastructure that powers AI training, customization and inference. Mistral is bringing additional NVIDIA-powered AI infrastructure online in support of Mistral’s compute roadmap targeting 1 GW of capacity by 2030. This expansion strengthens Europe’s role in developing and delivering AI for the world. By connecting European infrastructure and research with open models, specialized engineering capabilities and customer applications, Mistral and NVIDIA are helping enterprises build AI around their own expertise and scale it to serve markets worldwide. 0%

item.title: Train Qwen3 on AWS Trainium with torchtitan
item.abstract: Using torchtitan on AWS Trainium means using it the way you always have. TorchNeuron registers Trainium as a native PyTorch device, which lets torchtitan use it through standard PyTorch interfaces. You can use these configurations to pre-train from random initialization or fine-tune published weights. You can also customize the model implementation and kernels for your workload. In this post, you train Qwen3 three ways on a single trn2.48xlarge . The first method uses Transformers v5 as a modeling backend in torchtitan. It runs Hub models through AutoModelForCausalLM and reads and writes published safetensors directly. The second method switches to torchtitan’s native Qwen3 by changing config.model_spec . The third adds Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) mixture-of-experts (MoE) kernels from the torchtitan-neuron recipes and then uses torchtitan’s override registry to attach your own kernel. All three configurations use the same torchrun launch pattern and config structure. To follow this walkthrough, use a single trn2.48xlarge with either the AWS Deep Learning AMI for Neuron or a Neuron PyTorch training container. Both environments provide the Neuron driver, runtime, and compiler required to train on Trainium. Before you install torchtitan-neuron , check whether your environment already includes it. The following command prints the installed version and package path: This walkthrough uses the versions in the following table. To reproduce the examples, pin these versions. The Transformers v5 integration and Trainium-specific override modules can change between torchtitan releases. When torch_neuronx is installed, TorchNeuron registers Trainium as the neuron device and torchtitan detects it at startup. In eager mode, Neuron compiles operations as they execute. With torch.compile , Neuron compiles the captured graph. This same launch pattern works across all three configurations. For the versions used in this walkthrough, install torchtitan-neuron and torchtitan’s remaining dependencies with --no-deps to preserve the Neuron build of torch: Before you start training, get the Qwen3 model artifacts from Hugging Face Hub. Store them in a local directory that you can pass to the training config: Each training configuration is a Python config function. The three examples start from a base config that you update for each step. In the first configuration, Transformers v5 builds Qwen3 through AutoModelForCausalLM . The Hub model definition supplies the implementation used for the forward and backward passes. You select the model by setting its Hub ID in the config. Start with transformers_modeling_backend_full() . It leaves the fields that map to Hugging Face configuration keys unset, so AutoConfig.from_pretrained() loads the model architecture from the Hub. Create neuron_qwen3.py in the torchtitan-neuron repository root, where you run the training command. Add the imports, model artifact path, and base config: This command launches 64 training processes, one for each logical NeuronCore. --module neuron_qwen3 imports the local config module. --config v5_qwen3_4b selects the configuration function. The data parallel setting shards the model across all 64 ranks. To fine-tune from published weights, enable checkpoint loading and point initial_load_path to ASSETS . The state-dictionary adapter adjusts the leading model. prefix and handles tied embeddings. It saves the final checkpoint as Hugging Face safetensors. Use the first training-step loss as a quick check that torchtitan loaded the published weights. For Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 , the verified run produced a step 1 loss of 6.54 from published weights and 12.43 from random initialization. After training, load the exported checkpoint with AutoModelForCausalLM and load_state_dict . A successful round trip reports no missing or unexpected keys other than lm_head.weight , which Qwen3-4B ties to the token embeddings. This confirms that the files remain a standard Hugging Face checkpoint. Add the native Qwen3 imports and config function to neuron_qwen3.py : This example starts from qwen3_32b() because the tested torchtitan build does not provide a generic qwen3_4b() config builder. The next line replaces the 32B model specification with the 4B specification. The remaining fields reproduce the tested run. config.model_spec selects the model class and defines how torchtitan shards the model and maps its checkpoint keys. Here, model_registry("4B", attn_backend="sdpa") selects torchtitan’s native Qwen3 implementation with scaled dot product attention (SDPA). In the third configuration, torchtitan runs mixture-of-experts layers with kernels written in NKI, the Neuron kernel language. Add the required imports and Qwen3 MoE config function to neuron_qwen3.py : This configuration uses data parallel sharding across 64 ranks with a tensor parallel degree of 1. It does not use expert parallelism. num_experts=64 sets the number of experts in the model, not the expert parallel degree. Setting CompileConfig(enable=False) runs this example in eager mode. TorchNeuron supports registered NKI operators in both eager execution and torch.compile . In the torchtitan build used for this walkthrough, qwen3_nki_moe_config() replaces the MoE block with the NKI grouped-experts implementation. It also selects SDPA and the gather-free rotary embedding. When you enable torch.compile , add "grad_clip" to CompileConfig.components to compile gradient-norm clipping. NKI kernels enter training as PyTorch operators. wrap_nki makes an NKI kernel callable from PyTorch, and nki_op registers the operator. register_autograd attaches its backward pass using routing metadata saved during the forward pass. The example reduces Qwen3-30B-A3B to 4 layers and 64 experts so it fits on one trn2.48xlarge . It routes each token to 4 experts with top_k=4 . In some cases, you might want to optimize an operation for the tensor shapes in your model. A specialized kernel can tailor its tiling and data movement to those shapes. item.title: While Amazon blocks AI agents, Walmart rolls out the welcome mat
item.abstract: Walmart is embracing agentic commerce with the launch of its own Agent Gateway to manage transactions and other new features aimed at customers using AI agents, the retailer announced on Wednesday. The move comes shortly after Walmart’s top competitor, Amazon, began blocking AI agents from making purchases on behalf of online shoppers. The company’s embrace of AI technology differentiates it from other online businesses, including not only Amazon but also various travel and booking sites, which have responded to the growing consumer adoption of AI agents by locking them out of their websites completely . Walmart, on the other hand, had already announced a partnership with a leading agent in the space, Meta’s Muse, and offers integrations with popular AI apps like ChatGPT, Gemini, and others. Now, it’s expanding on those efforts with more technology to prepare for a world where AI agents become mainstream, said Walmart President and CEO John Furner, speaking at the Masters of Scale Summit in San Francisco on Wednesday. The technology will support agentic shopping from both Walmart and the company’s discount warehouse, Sam’s Club. It starts with Walmart’s Agent Gateway, the company’s new MCP server, which is designed to help approved agents connect to Walmart over the model context protocol (MCP). The protocol, originally created by Anthropic, allows AI agents to connect to external data sources, tools, and other workflows. In this case, it lets an AI agent search across Walmart’s online inventory and make purchases on behalf of the agent’s user. What’s more, the retailer says that its Agent Gateway will be able to help customers shop for their usual brands or items without having to share their personal information or purchase history directly with the agent. The company has also developed new technology to differentiate an agent’s purchases from those initiated directly by the customer, and to give shoppers more control over what their agents can and cannot do. With Agent Profiles, rolling out next month, customers will be able to authorize each AI agent they use with a dedicated profile in their account, allowing them to see the agent’s purchases separately from their own. Plus, customers will be in control of how purchases get approved by either requiring approval for each transaction or by authorizing transactions within a certain spending limit they set. The retailer says these controls are similar to adding someone as an authorized user on your credit card, where their transactions are identified, and you can cap their spending. The Agent Profiles will be created the first time you use a given agent to shop through the Walmart Agent Gateway, the company notes. To get started, you’ll authorize and link the Agent Profile to your Walmart account, then set your controls or spending limits. You can also delete an Agent Profile at any time. Agent support is available for anyone with a Walmart account; a Walmart+ membership is not necessary. Alongside these technologies, Walmart is introducing special “terms” for AI agents, which specify how they must operate and what rights they have to transact on its site. Of note, Walmart says that its returns process applies, including when an agent doesn’t act as intended. That’s a customer-friendly condition that could sway consumers who were worried about being an early tester of agentic commerce, as they won’t fear ending up with products they don’t want because of a misbehaving agent. Walmart also says that agents can’t take actions beyond what the shopper intends, can’t access the customers’ payment information, and can only access the information they need for the given task. Agents that don’t comply with the terms will be blocked from accessing Walmart’s site.

item.title: ✅China’s Draft AI Export Controls Don’t Block Open-Weight Models
item.abstract: On October 16, China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) released a draft addition to the country’s catalogue of technologies restricted or prohibited from export. For the first time , the proposal covers advanced large AI models, AI agents and massive computing clusters. Anything on the list would either be barred from leaving China or require a license. The draft names 40 key technologies across AI, biopharma and photovoltaic technologies (used to manufacture solar panels). 14 are prohibited while 26 are restricted and would need permission to export. The ministries are taking public comment from Oct 16 to Nov 15, therefore this is a draft, not a final rule. While the draft is under consultation, a temporary registration is required for exports of the listed technologies, including transactions underway but not yet completed. It covers overseas ownership transfers and licensing, as well as changes that place domestically held technology under foreign ownership or actual control. You can find the original Chinese text here. The Geopolitechs newsletter published an insightful analysis ended with a few great open questions. In this issue, I’ll focus primarily on the listed AI models, agents and computing infrastructure and debunk some myths circulating on social media. The prohibited AI technologies covers models trained using China’s legally designated “core data,” which refers to data involving national security, the lifelines of the national economy, major aspects of people's livelihoods, or major public interests. Also prohibited from export are agents for highly sensitive applications (like national defense and military), advanced offensive cyber technologies featuring AI-driven malware generation and mutation , and certain deepfake-detection technologies for cross-border data security. Models trained on “important data” fall into the restricted category, subject to exceptions. This compromise of important data could endanger national security, economic operations, social stability, or public interests. So does any model that meets one of three thresholds: Training computation ≥10²⁶ floating-point operations . Globally leading capability, defined through top-10 public assessments at the time of export. Those assessments can include specialized capabilities, usage, safety, or training efficiency—not just overall performance. Covered technologies include weights, checkpoints, source code, architecture, and training and inference optimizations. Agents are judged on autonomy and intended use. Restricted agents include systems meeting combined thresholds for decomposing tasks into at least 20 steps, coordinating at least 60 agents, or integrating at least 200 tools, alongside specified accuracy, efficiency, and success rates. Advanced strategic decision-making agents are also covered. Other restricted AI-related technologies include AI and memory-chip design, computing systems with more than 10,000 AI accelerator cards, AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation, and advanced detection, voiceprint recognition, and translation. The draft adds two explicit footnotes. First, technology already in the public domain through open source, academic publication, or similar means is outside the export controls’ scope. Second, for restricted AI technologies , open-source release, Chinese companies’ self-built and self-operated overseas computing centers, overseas chip fabrication, joint R&D using overseas resources, and international standards work would receive automatic licensing or other facilitation .
